lead: Sampling distributions describe how a statistic moves from sample to sample. This unit shows how to use them to judge estimators, find maximum likelihood estimates, and report confidence intervals for means and variances. After it you can choose a sensible estimator, check its bias and consistency, and state a 95% confidence interval in plain language.
about: The unit begins with population, sample and statistic, then shows how a statistic such as the sample mean varies from sample to sample. Chapter 5.2 gives the sampling distribution of the mean and variance, including standard error and the normal and chi-square links. Chapter 5.3 defines the chi-square, t and F distributions that arise from normal samples. Chapter 5.4 judges point estimators by bias, variance, mean squared error and consistency. Chapter 5.5 finds maximum likelihood estimates, and Chapter 5.6 turns an estimate plus its standard error into a confidence interval. The chapters build in that order: each later chapter uses the sampling distribution and estimator ideas from the earlier ones.

chapters.idea: A statistic is a function of a sample, and random sampling gives it a sampling distribution.
chapters.depth: Define population (all units under study, size N), sample (selected units, size n), parameter (a fixed population value such as μ) and statistic (a function of sample values only). Simple random sampling gives every sample of size n the same chance; cover with replacement and without replacement. The sampling distribution of a statistic is its probability distribution over repeated samples. Define standard error as the standard deviation of that distribution. Distinguish sampling error from non-sampling error. Some syllabi call a statistic a sample statistic.

figure.title: From population to sampling distribution
figure.aria: Flow from a four-value population through all six samples of size two to the sample mean and its distribution.

chapters.example: A population has four daily UPI transaction amounts, in hundreds of rupees: 2, 4, 6 and 8. List every simple random sample of size n = 2 without replacement, compute the sample mean x̄ for each, and form its sampling distribution. μ = (2+4+6+8)/4 = 5 and σ² = [(2−5)²+(4−5)²+(6−5)²+(8−5)²]/4 = 5. The six samples and their means are (2,4)→3, (2,6)→4, (2,8)→5, (4,6)→5, (4,8)→6, (6,8)→7. Each sample has probability 1/6. So P(x̄=3)=1/6, P(x̄=4)=1/6, P(x̄=5)=2/6, P(x̄=6)=1/6, P(x̄=7)=1/6. The mean of this distribution is (3+4+5+5+6+7)/6 = 5 = μ.
chapters.trap: Confusing a parameter with a statistic, or writing a statistic that contains the unknown parameter.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 probability basics; Unit 1 data summaries.
chapters.leave: Leave probability axioms to Unit 2, data summaries to Unit 1, and hypothesis tests to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The sample mean and sample variance have their own distributions, centred on the population values.
chapters.depth: Define the sample mean x̄ = (ΣXi)/n and sample variance S² = Σ(Xi−x̄)²/(n−1). For a random sample from a population with mean μ and variance σ², E(x̄)=μ and Var(x̄)=σ²/n; the standard error is σ/√n, estimated by s/√n. By the central limit theorem, x̄ is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) for large n; for a normal population it is exact for every n. For a normal population, (n−1)S²/σ² has a chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom (df), and x̄ and S² are independent. Mention finite population correction as an extension only.

figure.aria: Normal curves for the sample mean when sigma is 10 and sample sizes are 4, 16 and 25; the curve narrows as n rises.

chapters.example: A normal population has mean μ = 50 and standard deviation σ = 10. A sample of n = 25 is drawn. Find P(46 ≤ x̄ ≤ 54). The standard error is σ/√n = 10/√25 = 2. Standardise: z = (46−50)/2 = −2 and z = (54−50)/2 = 2. From the standard normal table, P(−2 ≤ Z ≤ 2) = 0.9544. So the probability is about 0.954, or 95.4%.
chapters.trap: Using s/√n in place of σ/√n without saying it is estimated, or treating x̄ as normal for small n from a non-normal population.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1; Unit 3 normal distribution; Unit 4 central limit theorem.
chapters.leave: Leave the proof of the central limit theorem to Unit 4, normal density properties to Unit 3, and tests to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Three distributions built from normal samples describe sample variances and ratios.
chapters.depth: Define χ² with ν degrees of freedom (df) as the distribution of Z1² + ... + Zν² for independent standard normal Z1,...,Zν; its mean is ν and variance is 2ν. Define t with ν df as Z/√(V/ν), where Z is standard normal, V is χ² with ν df, and they are independent; it is symmetric and has heavier tails than normal. Define F with (ν1,ν2) df as (U/ν1)/(V/ν2) for independent chi-squares U and V; it is positive and skewed. Give uses: t for means with unknown σ, χ² for variance and goodness of fit, F for variance ratios and ANOVA. Some syllabi call t the Student's t distribution.

figure.title: How t and F are built
figure.aria: A standard normal and a chi-square with 10 df form t with 10 df; chi-squares with 5 and 10 df form F with 5 and 10 df.

chapters.example: Take Z ~ N(0,1) and V ~ χ² with ν = 10 df, independent. Then T = Z/√(V/10) has a t distribution with 10 df. From the t table, P(T ≤ 1.812) = 0.95. Also, if U ~ χ² with 5 df and W ~ χ² with 10 df are independent, F = (U/5)/(W/10) has an F distribution with (5,10) df; the upper 5% point is F = 3.33.
chapters.trap: Mixing degrees of freedom, using t when σ is known, or reversing the numerator and denominator in an F ratio.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 normal distribution; Unit 2 random variables; Chapter 5.2 sampling distributions.
chapters.leave: Leave t-tests, F-tests, chi-square tests and ANOVA procedures to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A point estimator is judged by bias, variance, mean squared error and consistency.
chapters.depth: An estimator T is a statistic used to guess a parameter θ; its observed value is an estimate. Bias is E(T)−θ; T is unbiased when bias is 0. Mean squared error is MSE(T)=Var(T)+[Bias(T)]². For two unbiased estimators, the one with smaller variance is more efficient. Tn is consistent for θ if Tn → θ in probability as n → ∞; a sufficient condition is bias → 0 and Var(Tn) → 0. Give standard results: x̄ is unbiased for μ; S² with denominator n−1 is unbiased for σ²; p̂ is unbiased for p; s is not unbiased for σ. Mention sufficiency only in one line if needed.

figure.title: Judging a point estimator
figure.aria: An estimator is checked for bias and variance, combined into mean squared error, then checked for consistency as sample size grows.

chapters.example: Using the population 2, 4, 6, 8 with σ² = 5, draw samples of size n = 2 without replacement. Compare T1 = x̄ and T2 = first observation. Both are unbiased: E(T1) = E(T2) = μ = 5. Var(T1) = (σ²/n)·((N−n)/(N−1)) = (5/2)·(2/3) = 5/3 ≈ 1.667. Var(T2) = σ² = 5. T1 has smaller variance, so it is more efficient. As n grows, Var(T1) → 0, so T1 is consistent.
chapters.trap: Saying unbiased means close for one sample, or ignoring that S² with n−1 is unbiased while the MLE variance with denominator n is biased.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1, Chapter 5.2; Unit 2 expectation and variance.
chapters.leave: Leave confidence intervals to Chapter 5.6 and test decisions to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The maximum likelihood estimate is the parameter value that makes the observed sample most likely.
chapters.depth: Let x1,...,xn be observed values from a distribution with unknown parameter θ. The likelihood is L(θ)=Π f(xi;θ), or Π P(X=xi;θ) in the discrete case. The maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) θ̂ is the value that maximises L(θ). Work with the log-likelihood ℓ(θ)=ln L(θ): take the derivative, set it to 0, solve, and check the second derivative or boundary. State invariance: if θ̂ is the MLE of θ, then g(θ̂) is the MLE of g(θ). List MLEs for Bernoulli, normal, Poisson and exponential. Note that an MLE can be biased.

figure.aria: Likelihood curve for p with seven successes in ten trials; the peak is at p = 0.7.

chapters.example: In 10 independent UPI payment attempts on a slow network, 7 succeed. Model the number of successes as Binomial(10, p). Find the maximum likelihood estimate of p. The likelihood is L(p) = C(10,7) p⁷ (1−p)³, where C(10,7) = 120 is the binomial coefficient. The constant does not affect the maximum. log L = constant + 7 ln p + 3 ln(1−p). Set d(log L)/dp = 7/p − 3/(1−p) = 0. Then 7(1−p) = 3p, so 10p = 7 and p̂ = 0.7. The second derivative is negative at p = 0.7, so this is a maximum.
chapters.trap: Dropping the constant is fine, but forgetting to check the maximum, or forgetting that an MLE can be biased.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 expectation; Unit 3 distributions; calculus derivatives; Chapter 5.4.
chapters.leave: Leave interval construction to Chapter 5.6 and numerical optimisation beyond one-parameter closed forms to advanced courses.

chapters.idea: A confidence interval is a random range that covers the parameter with a stated long-run probability.
chapters.depth: An interval estimator gives random lower and upper limits; the confidence coefficient 1−α is the long-run fraction of intervals that contain the parameter, where α is the tail probability. For a normal population with known σ, use x̄ ± z(α/2) σ/√n, where z(α/2) cuts off tail area α/2. With unknown σ, use x̄ ± t(α/2,n−1) s/√n; this is exact for a normal population and approximate for large n. For variance, use (n−1)s²/χ²(α/2,n−1) to (n−1)s²/χ²(1−α/2,n−1). For a large-sample proportion, use p̂ ± z(α/2)√(p̂(1−p̂)/n). Explain margin of error, sample size and correct coverage wording. Some syllabi call this an interval estimate.

figure.title: Building a confidence interval
figure.aria: Sample data gives a point estimate, then a standard error, then a critical value, then the margin of error and the interval.

chapters.example: A random sample of n = 16 from a normal population gives x̄ = 52 and s = 8. Population σ is unknown. Find a 95% confidence interval for μ. Degrees of freedom = n−1 = 15. From the t table, t(0.975,15) = 2.131. Standard error = s/√n = 8/4 = 2. Margin of error = 2.131 × 2 = 4.262. The interval is 52 ± 4.262, that is (47.74, 56.26).
chapters.trap: Using z instead of t when σ is unknown and n is small, or saying the observed interval has 95% probability to contain μ.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.2, Chapter 5.3, Chapter 5.4, Chapter 5.5; Unit 3 normal distribution.
chapters.leave: Leave hypothesis testing, p-values and test procedures to Unit 6.
